title: Choosing Adaptation & Dataset Curation
scopeHtml: Scope: Prompt vs RAG vs fine-tuning, dataset quality, instruction data formats and preference datasets.

notes.title: The three adaptation levers in plain words
notes.html:
A base large language model (LLM) is a program that predicts the next token (a token is a small chunk of text, roughly three quarters of an English word). Out of the box it knows a lot about the public internet up to its training cutoff and nothing about your company. Adaptation means making that general model useful for one specific job. There are three main levers, and a fourth (tools) that is often confused with them.

Lever What you change When the change takes effect Typical effort
Prompting The text you send: instructions, examples, format rules Every single request Minutes, no training
RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) Which documents are looked up and pasted into the prompt Every request, from an index you maintain Days to build, minutes to update content
Fine-tuning The model's weights, by training on example conversations Permanently, until you retrain Days to weeks including data and eval
Tools / function calling Which live systems the model may call Every request Engineering work

Why three levers exist: they fix different kinds of failure. A model can fail because it does not know something (missing facts), because it does not behave the way you want (wrong format, tone, or skill), or because it cannot act (no live data). Matching the lever to the failure is the single most valuable skill in this topic, and mismatching them is the most common waste of money in applied GenAI.

Real products show all three. GitHub Copilot style assistants use prompting plus retrieval of nearby code. Customer-support bots at most SaaS companies use RAG over help-center articles. Bloomberg trained BloombergGPT from scratch on financial text, and many companies fine-tune open-weight models such as Llama or Mistral to emit a strict JSON dialect cheaply. OpenAI, Google Vertex AI and open-source stacks such as Hugging Face TRL all expose fine-tuning APIs or libraries (check each vendor's current docs for which models are tunable, this changes often, verify).

Everyday analogy, after the explanation: you hire a smart new employee. Prompting is the instruction sheet you hand them each morning. RAG is the filing cabinet they can open while working. Fine-tuning is sending them on a training course so the skill is in their head. Tools are the phone and the company laptop.

See also (existing notes): 01_W1 covers the high-level decision and the build-the-eval-first rule, and 02_P1 covers LoRA and QLoRA mechanics. This note goes deeper on the choice procedure, the data curation pipeline, training-example formats and preference data.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "fine-tuning teaches the model new facts" as a blanket truth. It can shift behaviour reliably; memorising facts is unreliable, hard to update and gives no citations.
  • Treating the levers as exclusive. Production systems usually combine them (fine-tuned behaviour, RAG for facts, tools for live data).
  • Forgetting that prompting is free to try. Any proposal to fine-tune without a prompting baseline is a red flag.

notes.title: A step-by-step procedure for choosing the method
notes.html:
Do not choose by taste. Run a short procedure, and let a measured gap justify each step up in complexity.

START: define the task + a small eval set (50-200 real examples, scored)
  |
  v
1. Best-effort PROMPT (clear instructions, 3-8 examples, output schema)
  |-- meets target? --> STOP, ship the prompt
  v
2. Diagnose the failures: sort 30 wrong answers into buckets
     A) missing/outdated/private facts   -> add RAG
     B) needs live data or actions       -> add TOOLS
     C) wrong style/format/skill         -> improve prompt, then FINE-TUNE
     D) model too weak at reasoning      -> bigger/better model, not tuning
  |
  v
3. Re-measure after each single change (change one thing at a time)
  |
  v
4. Fine-tune only if bucket C remains AND you can get quality data
  |
  v
5. Re-run the same eval on the tuned model; compare cost and latency too

The diagnosis step is the heart. Suppose you have an insurance-claims assistant. Out of 30 bad answers, 18 quote a policy clause that changed last month (bucket A, retrieval of current policy text fixes it), 7 produce malformed JSON the downstream system rejects (bucket C, a stricter prompt plus a fine-tune may help), 3 need the claim's live status (bucket B, a tool) and 2 are plain arithmetic errors (bucket D). The majority is a knowledge problem, so fine-tuning would have been the wrong first investment even though it feels like the "serious" option.

A decision function, written as code so the logic is explicit. It takes the bucket counts from your failure analysis and recommends the next move.

from collections import Counter

def next_move(failures: Counter, prompt_tried: bool) -> str:
    # failures keys: "facts", "live", "style", "reasoning"
    if not prompt_tried:
        return "write a best-effort prompt with examples first"
    top, _ = failures.most_common(1)[0]
    return {
        "facts": "add RAG over current documents",
        "live": "add a tool / function call",
        "style": "improve prompt; if still failing, fine-tune",
        "reasoning": "try a stronger model; tuning rarely fixes this",
    }[top]

# prints: add RAG over current documents
print(next_move(Counter(facts=18, style=7, live=3, reasoning=2), True))
fun nextMove(failures: Map<String, Int>, promptTried: Boolean): String {
    if (!promptTried) return "write a best-effort prompt with examples first"
    val top = failures.maxByOrNull { it.value }!!.key
    return when (top) {
        "facts" -> "add RAG over current documents"
        "live" -> "add a tool / function call"
        "style" -> "improve prompt; if still failing, fine-tune"
        else -> "try a stronger model; tuning rarely fixes this"
    }
}

// prints: add RAG over current documents
fun main() = println(nextMove(mapOf("facts" to 18, "style" to 7, "live" to 3, "reasoning" to 2), true))
import java.util.Map;

public class NextMove {
    static String nextMove(Map<String, Integer> failures, boolean promptTried) {
        if (!promptTried) return "write a best-effort prompt with examples first";
        String top = failures.entrySet().stream()
            .max(Map.Entry.comparingByValue()).get().getKey();
        return switch (top) {
            case "facts" -> "add RAG over current documents";
            case "live" -> "add a tool / function call";
            case "style" -> "improve prompt; if still failing, fine-tune";
            default -> "try a stronger model; tuning rarely fixes this";
        };
    }

    public static void main(String[] a) {
        // prints: add RAG over current documents
        System.out.println(nextMove(Map.of("facts", 18, "style", 7, "live", 3, "reasoning", 2), true));
    }
}

Real-world note: teams at companies such as Stripe, Notion and Shopify have described (in public talks and blog posts, verify specifics) starting with prompts and retrieval and adding tuning only for narrow, high-volume tasks. The pattern is consistent even when the products differ.

Analogy after the explanation: a doctor does not operate first. They try advice, then medicine, then physiotherapy, and only operate when the cheaper steps are measured to fail.

Common interview traps.

  • Skipping the failure-bucket analysis and answering "fine-tune" by default.
  • Changing prompt, retriever and model in one go, so you cannot tell what helped.
  • Using fine-tuning to patch a weak base model's reasoning. Tuning shifts behaviour; it rarely adds capability a model does not have.
  • Not counting the cost of maintaining the choice (re-indexing for RAG, retraining for fine-tuning).

notes.title: Cost, latency and break-even maths
notes.html:
Beginners often compare methods on quality only. Seniors also compare cost per call, latency and maintenance. The classic case is a long few-shot prompt versus a fine-tuned small model.

Worked example (all prices are illustrative placeholders, verify current vendor pricing): a classifier prompt carries 1,500 tokens of instructions and examples, plus a 100-token user input, so 1,600 input tokens per call. Volume is 1,000,000 calls per month.

Prompted large model
  input tokens/month = 1,600 x 1,000,000 = 1.6 billion
  at an assumed $1.00 per million input tokens:
  1,600 million x $1.00 / 1M = $1,600 per month

Fine-tuned small model (examples baked into weights)
  input tokens/call = 100 (just the user input)
  input tokens/month = 100 x 1,000,000 = 0.1 billion
  at an assumed $0.30 per million (small model): 100 x $0.30 = $30 per month

Saving per month = $1,600 - $30 = $1,570
One-off cost (data labelling + training + eval) assumed $6,000
Break-even = $6,000 / $1,570 = about 3.8 months

Three lessons hide in that arithmetic. First, the saving scales with call volume, so at 10,000 calls per month the same project never pays back (saving about $15.7 per month, break-even over 30 years). Second, a hosted fine-tuned model may carry a higher per-token price or a hosting fee than the base, which can erase the saving (verify with the vendor). Third, prompt caching (offered by several providers, verify) can shrink the long-prompt cost, which narrows the gap. Always re-run the numbers with caching in mind.

Latency works similarly. Output speed depends mainly on model size, and the time to first token grows with prompt length. A smaller tuned model with a 100-token prompt answers faster than a large model reading 1,600 tokens, which matters for autocomplete and voice. RAG adds a retrieval hop (an embedding call plus a vector search, often tens to a few hundred milliseconds, measure yours).

A small helper to compute break-even keeps the discussion honest.

def break_even_months(calls, prompt_tok, tuned_tok, price_big, price_small, one_off):
    big = calls * prompt_tok / 1e6 * price_big       # $/month, prompted
    small = calls * tuned_tok / 1e6 * price_small    # $/month, tuned
    saving = big - small
    return float("inf") if saving <= 0 else one_off / saving

# prints about 3.82
print(round(break_even_months(1_000_000, 1600, 100, 1.00, 0.30, 6000), 2))
fun breakEvenMonths(calls: Double, promptTok: Double, tunedTok: Double,
                    priceBig: Double, priceSmall: Double, oneOff: Double): Double {
    val saving = calls * promptTok / 1e6 * priceBig - calls * tunedTok / 1e6 * priceSmall
    return if (saving <= 0) Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY else oneOff / saving
}

// prints about 3.82
fun main() = println(breakEvenMonths(1e6, 1600.0, 100.0, 1.0, 0.3, 6000.0))
public class BreakEven {
    static double months(double calls, double promptTok, double tunedTok,
                         double priceBig, double priceSmall, double oneOff) {
        double saving = calls * promptTok / 1e6 * priceBig - calls * tunedTok / 1e6 * priceSmall;
        return saving <= 0 ? Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY : oneOff / saving;
    }

    public static void main(String[] a) {
        // prints about 3.82
        System.out.println(months(1e6, 1600, 100, 1.0, 0.3, 6000));
    }
}

Analogy after the explanation: buying a coffee machine versus buying coffee daily. The machine only wins if you drink enough coffee, and you must count the maintenance.

Common interview traps.

  • Quoting a break-even number without volume, price assumptions and one-off costs.
  • Ignoring that prompt caching and cheaper small models reduce the benefit of tuning.
  • Forgetting the ongoing cost of retraining when the task or data changes.

notes.title: What dataset curation means and why quality dominates
notes.html:
Dataset curation is the work of collecting, cleaning, selecting, labelling and organising training examples so that the model learns the behaviour you want and nothing else. The phrase to remember: a fine-tuned model is a compressed copy of its data. If the data contains mistakes, inconsistent styles or leaked secrets, the model learns and repeats them, confidently.

Evidence for quality over quantity is widely cited. The LIMA paper (Meta, 2023, "LIMA: Less Is More for Alignment") reported strong instruction-following from roughly one thousand carefully chosen examples, supporting the "superficial alignment" idea that most knowledge comes from pretraining and tuning mostly teaches format and style. Other work, such as the Alpaca-era datasets of tens of thousands of machine-generated examples, showed that volume with uneven quality gives uneven results. Treat these as principles rather than guarantees: complex new skills (a niche programming language, medical coding) can still need many thousands of examples.

A practical curation pipeline:

Raw sources                 Steps                              Output
-----------                 -----                              ------
production logs  --+
expert-written    --+--> 1 collect --> 2 clean/normalise
synthetic (LLM)   --+        |             |
public datasets   --+        v             v
                         3 remove PII   4 dedupe (exact + near)
                             |             |
                             v             v
                         5 filter quality (rules + judge + humans)
                             |
                             v
                         6 balance + diversify (topics, lengths, edge cases)
                             |
                             v
                         7 split by group (train / validation / test)
                             |
                             v
                         8 version + document (data card) --> training set

Sources, ranked by how well they match real use. Production logs reflect the true input distribution, but need consent, filtering for good outcomes and anonymisation. Expert demonstrations (a nurse writing ideal triage summaries) are accurate but expensive. User corrections (the edit a human made to an AI draft) are gold because they point exactly at the model's mistakes. Synthetic data (a stronger model writes examples from seed tasks) is cheap and scalable, but must be filtered and mixed with real data; training a model only on another model's output risks copying that model's errors and narrowing diversity (sometimes called model collapse when repeated over generations, a research topic, verify details). Public datasets need licence checks: some forbid commercial use, and terms of service of some model providers restrict using their outputs to train competing models (read the terms).

Real-world: the Open Assistant project crowd-sourced human conversations; Databricks released Dolly 15k written by employees; many 2024-2025 open models rely heavily on curated plus synthetic data with strong filtering (Hugging Face's FineWeb-Edu used a classifier to keep educational pages, verify details). The common thread is aggressive selection.

Analogy after the explanation: a cookbook for a new chef. Ten tested recipes beat a thousand untested ones, and one recipe with salt where sugar belongs will be copied faithfully.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming "more data is always better". Noisy volume often hurts; a small clean set is a legitimate starting point.
  • Training on raw production logs without filtering for outcome quality, so you teach the model the old bot's mistakes.
  • Forgetting legal and privacy review (consent, PII, licences, provider terms).
  • Using synthetic data with no validation step and no real-data share.

notes.title: Cleaning, deduplication and filtering in code
notes.html:
Cleaning has three layers: cheap rules, statistical or model-based scoring, and human audit. Start with rules because they catch embarrassing problems for free.

Rule-based checks that nearly every project needs:

  • Drop empty or very short answers, and answers that are cut off (no final punctuation or a truncation marker).
  • Drop examples where the answer repeats the prompt, contains "As an AI language model" boilerplate, or contains refusals that are inappropriate for your task.
  • Detect and remove PII (emails, phone numbers, API keys) with regexes plus a dedicated tool such as Microsoft Presidio (verify current version).
  • Check format validity: if the target is JSON, parse it; if it is code, compile or run tests.
  • Normalise whitespace and Unicode so that "same" examples really match.

Deduplication matters because duplicates make the model memorise and inflate evaluation scores when copies land in both train and test. Exact dedup hashes the normalised text. Near-duplicate detection catches rewordings, commonly with MinHash plus locality-sensitive hashing (LSH), or with embedding similarity above a threshold. Exact dedup in three languages:

import hashlib, json, re

def norm(s: str) -> str:
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", s.strip().lower())

def dedupe(rows):
    seen, out = set(), []
    for r in rows:
        key = hashlib.sha256(norm(r["prompt"]).encode()).hexdigest()
        if key not in seen:
            seen.add(key)
            out.append(r)
    return out

rows = [{"prompt": "Reset  my password", "answer": "..."},
        {"prompt": "reset my password ", "answer": "..."}]
print(len(dedupe(rows)))  # prints 1
import java.security.MessageDigest

fun norm(s: String) = s.trim().lowercase().replace(Regex("\\s+"), " ")

fun sha256(s: String) = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")
    .digest(s.toByteArray()).joinToString("") { "%02x".format(it) }

fun dedupe(rows: List<Map<String, String>>): List<Map<String, String>> {
    val seen = HashSet<String>()
    return rows.filter { seen.add(sha256(norm(it.getValue("prompt")))) }
}

fun main() {
    val rows = listOf(mapOf("prompt" to "Reset  my password", "answer" to "..."),
                      mapOf("prompt" to "reset my password ", "answer" to "..."))
    println(dedupe(rows).size) // prints 1
}
import java.security.MessageDigest;
import java.util.*;

public class Dedupe {
    static String norm(String s) { return s.strip().toLowerCase().replaceAll("\\s+", " "); }

    static String sha256(String s) throws Exception {
        byte[] d = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(s.getBytes());
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (byte b : d) sb.append(String.format("%02x", b));
        return sb.toString();
    }

    public static void main(String[] a) throws Exception {
        List<String> prompts = List.of("Reset  my password", "reset my password ");
        Set<String> seen = new HashSet<>();
        int kept = 0;
        for (String p : prompts) if (seen.add(sha256(norm(p)))) kept++;
        System.out.println(kept); // prints 1
    }
}

For quality scoring beyond rules, teams use an LLM-as-judge: a strong model rates each example on a rubric (correctness, helpfulness, format) and low scorers are dropped or sent to humans. Judges have biases (they favour longer answers and their own style), so calibrate them against a human-labelled sample before trusting them, and spot-check a random 50 to 100 rejected and accepted rows each round. Tools in this space include Argilla and Label Studio for annotation and Hugging Face datasets plus distilabel for synthetic pipelines (verify current features).

Production failure patterns: a regex that strips "weird" characters also deletes non-English text or code symbols; an aggressive length filter removes all short, correct answers and biases the model toward verbosity; dedup on the answer only keeps ten different questions with the same boilerplate reply.

Analogy after the explanation: sorting rice before cooking. First a sieve for stones (rules), then a quick look for discoloured grains (judge), then a person checking a handful from each bag (audit).

Common interview traps.

  • Deduplicating after splitting. Do it before, otherwise copies can sit on both sides.
  • Trusting an LLM judge without calibrating on human labels.
  • Cleaning rules that silently remove an entire class (a language, short answers, refusals you actually want).
  • Not logging how many rows each filter removed, which makes pipeline bugs invisible.

notes.title: Diversity, balance, contamination and honest splits
notes.html:
After cleaning, the set must be representative. Check the distribution of topics, intents, input lengths, languages, difficulty and outcome types (including "I don't know", refusals and tool errors). A model trained on 95 percent easy "happy path" cases will perform badly on the 5 percent of hard ones that cause incidents. A simple method: cluster prompts by embedding (for example k-means with k around 20 to 50), count rows per cluster, and sample so no cluster dominates while rare clusters are kept.

Balance is a judgement call. For a classifier with classes in a 95:5 ratio, you may upsample the rare class for training but must evaluate on the natural distribution. For an assistant, keep a share of "negative" examples: unanswerable questions answered with "I don't know" teach honesty and reduce hallucination; ambiguous questions answered with a clarifying question teach good behaviour.

Data contamination (also called leakage) means test material appears in training. Two forms: your own test set leaking into train (duplicates, same customer, same document), and public benchmark questions leaking in from scraped or synthetic data, which inflates reported scores. Defences: dedupe train against test using the same near-duplicate method; split by group (customer id, document id, conversation id) instead of by row, so all rows from one group stay on one side; and check n-gram overlap against public benchmarks you plan to quote.

Split arithmetic example: you have 5,000 support conversations from 400 customers. A random row split puts the same customer's repeated wording on both sides, and the test score looks great but is optimistic. A group split by customer assigns, say, 320 customers (80 percent) to train, 40 to validation and 40 to test. Each split then measures generalisation to people the model has never seen. Keep the test set frozen: if you tweak the data each time you see test errors, the test set becomes a training signal (this is "overfitting to the test set").

import random
from collections import defaultdict

def group_split(rows, key="customer", ratios=(0.8, 0.1, 0.1), seed=7):
    groups = defaultdict(list)
    for r in rows:
        groups[r[key]].append(r)
    ids = sorted(groups)
    random.Random(seed).shuffle(ids)
    n = len(ids)
    a, b = int(n * ratios[0]), int(n * (ratios[0] + ratios[1]))
    pick = lambda part: [r for g in part for r in groups[g]]
    return pick(ids[:a]), pick(ids[a:b]), pick(ids[b:])
# returns (train, validation, test) with no customer in two splits
import kotlin.random.Random

fun groupSplit(rows: List<Map<String, String>>, key: String = "customer", seed: Int = 7):
        Triple<List<Map<String, String>>, List<Map<String, String>>, List<Map<String, String>>> {
    val groups = rows.groupBy { it.getValue(key) }
    val ids = groups.keys.sorted().shuffled(Random(seed))
    val a = (ids.size * 0.8).toInt()
    val b = (ids.size * 0.9).toInt()
    fun pick(part: List<String>) = part.flatMap { groups.getValue(it) }
    return Triple(pick(ids.subList(0, a)), pick(ids.subList(a, b)), pick(ids.subList(b, ids.size)))
}
// returns (train, validation, test) with no customer in two splits
import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class GroupSplit {
    // Splits group ids 80/10/10; rows are then collected per id set.
    static List<Set<String>> splitIds(Collection<String> groupIds, long seed) {
        List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>(new TreeSet<>(groupIds));
        Collections.shuffle(ids, new Random(seed));
        int a = (int) (ids.size() * 0.8), b = (int) (ids.size() * 0.9);
        return List.of(new HashSet<>(ids.subList(0, a)),
                       new HashSet<>(ids.subList(a, b)),
                       new HashSet<>(ids.subList(b, ids.size())));
    }
    // Usage: filter rows with ids.contains(row.customer()) for each returned set.
}

Analogy after the explanation: a driving test. If the examiner uses the same road you practised on every day, a pass tells you nothing about a new city.

Common interview traps.

  • Random row splits when rows are grouped (customers, documents, conversations).
  • Reporting a benchmark score without checking that benchmark text is absent from training data.
  • Rebalancing the test set; evaluate on the natural distribution you will meet in production.
  • Tuning the data repeatedly against one test set until it stops being independent.

notes.title: Annotation, labelling guidelines and agreement
notes.html:
When humans label or write data, the quality of the guideline matters as much as the people. A good guideline defines each label with 3 to 5 examples and counter-examples, covers edge cases ("what if the answer is partly correct?"), states style rules (tone, length, citations) and explains what to do when unsure (skip and flag, do not guess).

Process that works: draft guidelines, label a pilot of 50 items with 3 annotators, compare, discuss disagreements, refine the guidelines, repeat until agreement is stable, then scale up with periodic audits.

Inter-annotator agreement measures consistency. Raw percent agreement is misleading because two people guessing on a two-class task agree half the time by chance. Cohen's kappa corrects for chance: kappa = (observed agreement - chance agreement) / (1 - chance agreement). Worked example: two annotators agree on 90 of 100 items (observed 0.90). Each says "good" about half the time, so chance agreement is 0.5. Kappa = (0.90 - 0.50) / (1 - 0.50) = 0.40 / 0.50 = 0.80, which is usually read as strong agreement (rules of thumb vary by field, verify). If observed were 0.60, kappa would be (0.60 - 0.50) / 0.50 = 0.20, a warning that the task or the guideline is unclear and the labels are mostly noise.

def cohen_kappa(a, b):
    n = len(a)
    labels = set(a) | set(b)
    po = sum(x == y for x, y in zip(a, b)) / n
    pe = sum((a.count(l) / n) * (b.count(l) / n) for l in labels)
    return (po - pe) / (1 - pe) if pe < 1 else 1.0

# prints 0.8 (90 of 100 agree, balanced labels)
a = ["good"] * 50 + ["bad"] * 50
b = ["good"] * 45 + ["bad"] * 5 + ["good"] * 5 + ["bad"] * 45
print(round(cohen_kappa(a, b), 2))
fun cohenKappa(a: List<String>, b: List<String>): Double {
    val n = a.size.toDouble()
    val po = a.zip(b).count { it.first == it.second } / n
    val labels = (a + b).toSet()
    val pe = labels.sumOf { l -> (a.count { it == l } / n) * (b.count { it == l } / n) }
    return if (pe < 1.0) (po - pe) / (1 - pe) else 1.0
}
// prints 0.8 for the same 90-of-100 example as the python block
import java.util.*;

public class Kappa {
    static double kappa(List<String> a, List<String> b) {
        double n = a.size();
        double po = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < a.size(); i++) if (a.get(i).equals(b.get(i))) po++;
        po /= n;
        Set<String> labels = new HashSet<>(a);
        labels.addAll(b);
        double pe = 0;
        for (String l : labels)
            pe += (Collections.frequency(a, l) / n) * (Collections.frequency(b, l) / n);
        return pe < 1 ? (po - pe) / (1 - pe) : 1.0;
    }
    // prints 0.8 for the same 90-of-100 example as the python block
}

Tooling: Label Studio, Argilla, Prodigy and Scale AI or Surge AI style vendor services. Frontier labs use expert contractors for demonstrations and rankings, and report that guideline quality and rater training are a major cost (public statements vary, verify specifics).

Failure patterns: raters under time pressure choose the longer answer; a single rater writes all examples and bakes in their personal style; guideline changes mid-project leave a mixed-label dataset with no version marker.

Analogy after the explanation: referees in a sport. Without a shared rulebook and practice sessions, two referees call the same play differently, and the players learn chaos.

Common interview traps.

  • Reporting raw agreement percentage without correcting for chance.
  • Single annotator for the whole dataset, so style bias is invisible.
  • Changing guidelines without versioning the labelled data.
  • Believing a high-agreement label is necessarily correct; raters can agree on a wrong rule.

notes.title: Instruction data formats: how a training example is structured
notes.html:
An instruction example pairs an input with the ideal output. During supervised fine-tuning (SFT), the model is trained to produce the output given the input, using the ordinary next-token loss. Formats differ in how they store this, and the format must be converted to the exact text layout the model expects.

Common storage formats (each line below is a JSON object in a JSONL file, which means one JSON record per line so large files can be streamed):

1) Alpaca style (single turn)
   {"instruction": "Summarise the text", "input": "<text>", "output": "<summary>"}

2) ShareGPT style (multi turn)
   {"conversations": [{"from": "human", "value": "Hi"},
                      {"from": "gpt", "value": "Hello! How can I help?"}]}

3) Chat messages style (OpenAI-compatible, also used by Hugging Face TRL)
   {"messages": [{"role": "system", "content": "You are a billing assistant."},
                 {"role": "user", "content": "Why was I charged twice?"},
                 {"role": "assistant", "content": "Let me check your invoices."}]}

4) Prompt/completion style (older, simple)
   {"prompt": "Q: ...\nA:", "completion": " ..."}

Today the messages format is the practical default because hosted fine-tuning APIs and Hugging Face tooling accept it (check the current docs of your provider for exact fields, verify). It also extends to tool calls: an assistant message can contain a tool-call object and a following tool message carries the result, so you can teach the model to call your API correctly.

Between the stored record and the training tokens sits the chat template. Each model family wraps turns with special tokens, for example ChatML-style <|im_start|>role ... <|im_end|> markers used by several models, while Llama and Mistral have their own layouts. The template is shipped in the tokenizer configuration, and Hugging Face exposes it as tokenizer.apply_chat_template(...). Rule: train with the same template you will use at inference. A mismatch (training on plain text, serving with the chat template) is a classic cause of a tuned model that behaves worse than the base.

Loss masking. In a conversation, you usually want the model to learn to produce assistant turns only, not to predict the system prompt or user text. Implementations set the label for masked tokens to -100 (the ignore index of PyTorch's cross-entropy loss, which Hugging Face uses), so those positions add zero loss. TRL's SFT trainer offers options such as training on completions only (verify the current parameter names in the docs). Without masking, the model spends capacity learning to imitate users and may echo user-style text.

Tokens :  [SYS] You are...  [USER] Why twice?  [ASSISTANT] Let me check  [EOS]
Labels :   -100  -100 -100   -100   -100 -100    ...tokens...  ...tokens... EOS
Loss   :    0     0    0      0      0    0        counted        counted  counted

Include the end-of-sequence marker in the assistant turn; without it the model never learns when to stop and rambles.

Design choices for the content itself: keep the system prompt in training identical to (or a shortened but consistent version of) the one used in production; vary phrasing of user inputs; include multi-turn examples if your product is a chat; include examples with no tool call when none is needed, otherwise the model overuses tools. Typical size guidance: starting with a few hundred well-made examples to see if behaviour moves is common, and a few thousand for stability, but treat these as rules of thumb and measure on your eval.

Analogy after the explanation: a script for an actor. The script marks whose line is whose; the actor only needs to learn their own lines, and the stage directions (the template) must be identical at rehearsal and on opening night.

Common interview traps.

  • Training on a different template from the one used at inference.
  • Forgetting loss masking, or masking the assistant turn by mistake so nothing is learned.
  • Omitting the end-of-turn token so generation never stops cleanly.
  • Mixing tool-calling and plain-answer examples without examples of "no tool needed".

notes.title: Writing and validating training files in three languages
notes.html:
Before you pay for training, validate the file. Hosted services reject malformed lines after a delay, and your own trainers may silently skip them. A validator checks: valid JSON per line, a messages list, allowed roles, the last message from the assistant, no empty content, and a token or character budget.

import json, sys

ROLES = {"system", "user", "assistant", "tool"}

def validate(path, max_chars=20000):
    bad = 0
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for i, line in enumerate(f, 1):
            try:
                msgs = json.loads(line)["messages"]
                assert msgs and msgs[-1]["role"] == "assistant"
                assert all(m["role"] in ROLES for m in msgs)
                assert all(m.get("content") or m.get("tool_calls") for m in msgs)
                assert sum(len(m.get("content") or "") for m in msgs) <= max_chars
            except Exception as e:
                bad += 1
                print(f"line {i}: {type(e).__name__}", file=sys.stderr)
    return bad  # prints nothing when the file is clean

def write_example(f, system, user, answer):
    rec = {"messages": [{"role": "system", "content": system},
                        {"role": "user", "content": user},
                        {"role": "assistant", "content": answer}]}
    f.write(json.dumps(rec, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper
import java.io.File

private val mapper = ObjectMapper()
private val roles = setOf("system", "user", "assistant", "tool")

fun validate(path: String): Int {
    var bad = 0
    File(path).useLines { lines ->
        lines.forEachIndexed { i, line ->
            val ok = runCatching {
                val msgs = mapper.readTree(line).get("messages")
                require(msgs != null && msgs.size() > 0)
                require(msgs.last().get("role").asText() == "assistant")
                msgs.forEach { require(it.get("role").asText() in roles) }
            }.isSuccess
            if (!ok) { bad++; System.err.println("line ${i + 1}: invalid") }
        }
    }
    return bad // prints nothing on stderr when the file is clean
}

fun exampleLine(system: String, user: String, answer: String): String =
    mapper.writeValueAsString(mapOf("messages" to listOf(
        mapOf("role" to "system", "content" to system),
        mapOf("role" to "user", "content" to user),
        mapOf("role" to "assistant", "content" to answer))))
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.JsonNode;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.*;

public class ValidateJsonl {
    static final ObjectMapper M = new ObjectMapper();
    static final Set<String> ROLES = Set.of("system", "user", "assistant", "tool");

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        List<String> lines = Files.readAllLines(Path.of(args[0]));
        int bad = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < lines.size(); i++) {
            try {
                JsonNode msgs = M.readTree(lines.get(i)).get("messages");
                if (msgs == null || msgs.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
                if (!"assistant".equals(msgs.get(msgs.size() - 1).get("role").asText()))
                    throw new IllegalArgumentException();
                for (JsonNode m : msgs)
                    if (!ROLES.contains(m.get("role").asText())) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
            } catch (Exception e) {
                bad++;
                System.err.println("line " + (i + 1) + ": invalid");
            }
        }
        System.out.println("invalid lines: " + bad); // prints 0 for a clean file
    }
}

Android note: training itself is server-side. If an Android app collects feedback (thumbs up, edited text) to build future data, send it to your own backend with the user's consent and strip personal data there; never ship vendor API keys in the app.

Failure patterns: a Windows tool writes a BOM or CRLF and the first line fails to parse; a trailing comma or an unescaped newline in a string breaks one line out of 20,000 and the whole upload is rejected; non-UTF-8 text corrupts characters; long examples are silently truncated by the trainer's max sequence length, cutting off the answer and teaching the model to stop mid-sentence.

Analogy after the explanation: a pre-flight checklist. Pilots do not discover a missing fuel cap in the air, and you should not discover a malformed line after paying for training.

Common interview traps.

  • Skipping validation and learning of errors from the provider after a long queue.
  • Ignoring the trainer's maximum sequence length, so answers are truncated.
  • Writing files with the wrong encoding or line endings.
  • Collecting user data for training without consent or PII removal.

notes.title: Preference datasets: teaching the model what "better" means
notes.html:
SFT shows the model one good answer. But for many behaviours (helpfulness, tone, safety, concision) there is no single correct answer; there are better and worse ones. A preference dataset captures this with comparisons: for a prompt, one response is chosen (preferred) and another is rejected. It exists because humans find it far easier and more consistent to say "A is better than B" than to write a perfect answer or give an absolute score.

A record in the common TRL layout (columns prompt, chosen, rejected):

{"prompt": "Explain what a mutex is to a beginner.",
 "chosen": "A mutex is a lock that lets only one thread use a resource at a time...",
 "rejected": "Mutex means mutual exclusion. See any OS textbook."}

Conversational variants store lists of messages in chosen and rejected. OpenAI's preference fine-tuning (direct preference optimisation, DPO, offered on some models) uses its own JSONL shape with an input plus preferred and non-preferred outputs (verify the current field names in the docs before building a converter). Public examples to study: Anthropic's HH-RLHF, OpenAI's early summarisation comparisons, UltraFeedback and Argilla's distilabel datasets (verify current availability).

How preference data is used:

  1. RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback): train a reward model on the comparisons so it scores answers, then optimise the LLM with a reinforcement-learning algorithm such as PPO against that reward (as in InstructGPT, 2022). Powerful but complex, with several models in memory.
  2. DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023): skip the explicit reward model and optimise the LLM directly on the pairs. The loss, per example, is: minus log of sigmoid of beta times ((log pi(chosen) minus log ref(chosen)) minus (log pi(rejected) minus log ref(rejected))). Here pi is the model being trained, ref is a frozen copy of the starting model, and beta (commonly around 0.1, tune it) controls how far the model may drift from the reference.
  3. Other variants: KTO (works with thumbs-up/down labels instead of pairs), IPO, ORPO, and RLAIF / Constitutional AI where an AI model, guided by written principles, produces the preference labels instead of humans.

Worked DPO number: let beta = 0.1. Suppose training has raised the log-probability of the chosen answer by 2.0 relative to the reference and lowered the rejected by 1.0. The inside term is 0.1 x (2.0 - (-1.0)) = 0.1 x 3.0 = 0.3. sigmoid(0.3) is about 0.574, so loss = -ln(0.574) is about 0.555. If the model were unchanged (both differences 0), the term is 0, sigmoid(0) = 0.5 and loss = -ln(0.5) = 0.693. Lower loss means the model prefers chosen over rejected more strongly than the reference does.

import math

def dpo_loss(logp_c, logp_r, ref_c, ref_r, beta=0.1):
    margin = beta * ((logp_c - ref_c) - (logp_r - ref_r))
    return -math.log(1 / (1 + math.exp(-margin)))

# chosen +2.0 vs ref, rejected -1.0 vs ref -> prints 0.555
print(round(dpo_loss(2.0, -1.0, 0.0, 0.0), 3))
# Real training uses a library such as Hugging Face TRL's DPOTrainer (verify current API).
import kotlin.math.exp
import kotlin.math.ln

fun dpoLoss(lc: Double, lr: Double, rc: Double, rr: Double, beta: Double = 0.1): Double {
    val margin = beta * ((lc - rc) - (lr - rr))
    return -ln(1 / (1 + exp(-margin)))
}

// prints about 0.555; training itself is server-side Python, so this only illustrates the maths
fun main() = println(dpoLoss(2.0, -1.0, 0.0, 0.0))
public class Dpo {
    static double loss(double lc, double lr, double rc, double rr, double beta) {
        double margin = beta * ((lc - rc) - (lr - rr));
        return -Math.log(1 / (1 + Math.exp(-margin)));
    }

    public static void main(String[] a) {
        // prints about 0.555; real training runs in Python on GPUs
        System.out.println(loss(2.0, -1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.1));
    }
}

Analogy after the explanation: a taste test. You cannot describe the perfect soup, but you can reliably say which of two bowls tastes better, and enough of those votes teach the chef the taste.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying DPO needs no reference model. It needs a frozen reference (or its log-probs precomputed); it only avoids the separate reward model and RL loop.
  • Confusing SFT data (one answer) with preference data (a comparison).
  • Believing preference tuning adds knowledge. It mainly shifts style, helpfulness and safety behaviour.
  • Forgetting that preference tuning is normally done after SFT, starting from the SFT model.

notes.title: Building good preference pairs and avoiding their pitfalls
notes.html:
The value of a preference dataset depends on how the two responses are produced and how the label is decided.

Where the pairs come from.

  • On-policy sampling: sample two or more answers from your current model for each prompt (different temperature or seed), then have humans or a judge pick the better. On-policy pairs match what the model actually produces, which is why they often train more effectively than pairs from a different model.
  • Best versus worst of N: sample N answers (say 4 to 8), score all, take the highest as chosen and the lowest (or a clearly worse one) as rejected. A larger quality gap gives a clearer signal; near-ties give a noisy one.
  • Edits as preferences: the user's corrected text is chosen, the model's original draft is rejected. Cheap and highly targeted.
  • Rule-based or verifiable pairs: for code or maths, the answer that passes tests or matches the verified result is chosen. This is the most trustworthy label source.
  • Constitution or AI feedback: a judge model applies written principles (harmlessness, honesty). Fast, but inherits judge bias.

Quality controls specific to preferences.

  • Make rejected answers plausible, not strawmen. If rejected is obviously absurd, the model learns nothing subtle.
  • Control for length bias: raters and judges often prefer longer answers, and DPO-style training can then drift toward verbosity. Check the average length of chosen versus rejected; if chosen is consistently 40 percent longer, rebalance or add length-controlled pairs.
  • Remove ties and low-confidence labels; measure rater agreement the same way as before (kappa above).
  • Keep the prompt distribution diverse and include safety cases (refusal quality, not blanket refusal).
  • Deduplicate and split by prompt, as with SFT.
  • Watch for reward hacking in RLHF-style setups: the model finds outputs that score high on the learned reward but are bad (flattery, hedging, formatting tricks).

A small builder that turns N scored samples into a pair, and drops weak margins, looks like this:

def make_pair(prompt, samples, min_gap=1.0):
    # samples: list of (text, score); returns a record or None when the gap is too small
    ranked = sorted(samples, key=lambda s: s[1], reverse=True)
    best, worst = ranked[0], ranked[-1]
    if best[1] - worst[1] < min_gap:
        return None
    return {"prompt": prompt, "chosen": best[0], "rejected": worst[0]}

# prints a record; with scores 4.5 and 2.0 the gap is 2.5 >= 1.0
print(make_pair("Explain a mutex", [("clear answer", 4.5), ("vague answer", 2.0), ("ok answer", 3.4)]))
data class Pref(val prompt: String, val chosen: String, val rejected: String)

fun makePair(prompt: String, samples: List<Pair<String, Double>>, minGap: Double = 1.0): Pref? {
    val ranked = samples.sortedByDescending { it.second }
    val best = ranked.first()
    val worst = ranked.last()
    return if (best.second - worst.second < minGap) null
    else Pref(prompt, best.first, worst.first)
}
// returns a Pref for scores 4.5 and 2.0 (gap 2.5), null when the gap is below 1.0
import java.util.*;

public class MakePair {
    record Sample(String text, double score) {}
    record Pref(String prompt, String chosen, String rejected) {}

    static Optional<Pref> makePair(String prompt, List<Sample> samples, double minGap) {
        List<Sample> r = new ArrayList<>(samples);
        r.sort(Comparator.comparingDouble(Sample::score).reversed());
        Sample best = r.get(0), worst = r.get(r.size() - 1);
        if (best.score() - worst.score() < minGap) return Optional.empty();
        return Optional.of(new Pref(prompt, best.text(), worst.text()));
    }
    // returns a Pref for scores 4.5 and 2.0 (gap 2.5), empty when the gap is below 1.0
}

Real-world: the InstructGPT and Llama 2 papers describe collecting human rankings of several sampled answers and training reward models; Llama 2 reports using multiple rounds of fresh comparisons as the model improved (details in the paper, verify). Zephyr (Hugging Face, 2023) popularised DPO on AI-scored UltraFeedback pairs for open models. Anthropic's Constitutional AI paper describes AI feedback guided by principles.

Failure patterns: the tuned model becomes preachy or over-refuses because the dataset rewarded refusals; verbosity creeps up; the model becomes sycophantic because raters liked agreement; quality regresses on tasks absent from preference prompts (sometimes called alignment tax, verify wording).

Analogy after the explanation: a judge at a talent show who always rewards the loudest act. After a few seasons every contestant shouts.

Common interview traps.

  • Using pairs where chosen and rejected differ in length or format more than in quality.
  • Using off-policy pairs and expecting on-policy gains.
  • Trusting an AI judge without checking its biases (length, position, self-preference).
  • Running preference tuning without an eval for the behaviours you did not want to change.

notes.title: Production failure patterns and a pre-training checklist
notes.html:
Pulling the topic together, these are the incidents that recur in real projects, with the symptom and the usual root cause.

Symptom after tuning Likely root cause Fix
Great on test set, bad in production Leakage or non-representative test Group split, sample real traffic for eval
Model hallucinates company facts confidently Facts were trained in via SFT instead of retrieved Move facts to RAG, tune only behaviour
Output format broken on edge inputs Training data lacked those edge cases Add edge cases, constrained decoding or schema validation
Model forgets general skills Too high learning rate, too many epochs, narrow data Lower rate, fewer epochs, mix in general data (see 02_P1)
Replies never stop or stop mid-sentence Missing end token, or truncation by max length Add EOS to the assistant turn, raise max length
Becomes verbose or sycophantic Preference data length and agreement bias Rebalance pairs, add length-controlled and disagreement examples
Leaks private data PII in training set PII scan before training, privacy review
Gets worse after a new data batch No versioning, label drift Version data and guidelines, run regression eval

Pre-training checklist (use it as a gate before spending GPU money):

  1. A frozen eval set, group-split, never used for tuning, plus a prompting baseline score.
  2. A data card: sources, licences, consent, filters applied, row counts after each filter, guideline version.
  3. Validator passed: schema, roles, end tokens, length budget, encoding.
  4. PII and secrets scan done; legal review of licences and provider terms.
  5. Chat template identical to inference; loss masking confirmed on one decoded example (print the tokens and labels and read them yourself).
  6. A small pilot run (a few hundred examples) showing the metric moves before scaling.
  7. A rollback plan: keep the base model and the previous tuned version deployable.

Also monitor after launch. Sample production outputs weekly, track the eval metrics over time, and feed corrected cases back into the next dataset version; this is the data flywheel that products such as GitHub Copilot and customer-support copilots rely on (as publicly described, verify specifics).

Analogy after the explanation: running a restaurant kitchen. The recipe (data) is written, tested in small batches, labelled with allergens (data card), and the last batch is kept in case the new recipe fails.

Common interview traps.

  • Declaring success from training loss alone. Loss going down says nothing about behaviour; evaluate on held-out tasks.
  • Having no data versioning, so a regression cannot be traced.
  • Not checking a decoded training example by eye (template and masking bugs hide here).
  • Treating fine-tuning as a one-off instead of an ongoing data process.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Choose the lever by diagnosing the failure: missing facts means RAG, live data or actions means tools, wrong behaviour or format means better prompts first and then fine-tuning, weak reasoning means a stronger model. Build the eval and a prompting baseline before anything else.
  • Fine-tuning pays off for narrow, high-volume tasks, consistent style, shorter prompts and smaller models; the break-even depends on volume (example: 1.6 billion prompt tokens per month, $1,570 saved against a $6,000 one-off cost gives about 3.8 months, with illustrative prices).
  • Dataset curation is the main quality lever: collect from matched sources, clean with rules and judges, remove PII, deduplicate exactly and approximately, balance and diversify, and split by group with a frozen test set.
  • Annotation needs clear guidelines, pilots and agreement metrics such as Cohen's kappa, which corrects for chance agreement.
  • Instruction data is usually stored as JSONL chat messages; use the model's chat template identical to inference, mask loss to assistant tokens (label -100), and include the end-of-turn token. Validate files before training.
  • Preference datasets store chosen versus rejected responses and feed RLHF reward models or DPO; the best pairs are on-policy with a clear quality gap, controlled for length and judge bias, and used after SFT.
  • Most production failures trace back to data: leakage, truncation, template mismatch, missing edge cases, bias and PII. Gate training with a checklist and keep the loop running after launch.

Common interview traps.

  • Answering "it depends" without naming the diagnostic that decides.
  • Quoting dataset sizes or prices as facts instead of rules of thumb to verify.
  • Forgetting that data, not the training algorithm, usually explains success or failure.
